extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, designers, and sculptors concerned with architectural ornament
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for choosing materials, expressing, arranging, and placing architectural ornament so it serves the building (not as independent sculpture). Advice covers specific materials (clouds, shells, foliage, animals), systems of ornament, and principles such as noble abstraction and executional feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of Air (clouds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cloud-forms are 'hardly more manageable than flames, and of no ornamental use, their majesty being in scale and color, and inimitable in marble.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating clouds as small-scale ornament; they belong to large-scale color/lighting effects and are generally unsuitable for detailed marble ornamentation, though some historic examples exist (e.g., Last Judgment at St. Maclou, Rouen; large flattened 'concretions' above altars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shells
rubrics_metrics.description: Shells rank low in material scale as 'moulds or coats of organism; not themselves organic' and convey a sense of emptiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shell forms sparingly. Prefer drawing the line of the shell rather than attempting full shell carving. Some shell forms (cockle/concha, scallop, crab grotesques) are appropriate in specific contexts (half-domes, symbol mixes), but avoid large or over-literal shell ornament that reads as hollow or deserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fish as ornamental material
rubrics_metrics.description: Fish are 'of great value as material of ornament'—often simple, plain-bodied forms are used in medieval work; some Greek types (dolphin) are picturesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select fish forms for their simple, supple outlines and symbolic meanings. Prefer plain-bodied medieval types for expression of water; capture characteristic action (e.g., revolving plunge of a dolphin) where appropriate to the medium and viewing distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reptiles and insects
rubrics_metrics.description: Serpents and lizards combine 'every element of beauty and horror' and are favorite subjects; the ideal dragon is highly picturesque and symbolically important in Christian art. Small frogs, lizards, snails, beetles, and various insects enliven sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the dramatic/symbolic potential of reptile and insect forms, but handle their horror and power deliberately so it reads as pleasurable excitement. Use smaller creatures to enliven foregrounds; reserve the most powerful reptile forms for places where their symbolism and pictorial power are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branches and stems of trees
rubrics_metrics.description: Branches and stems belong to a peculiar, imitative, luxuriant architecture and are 'only applicable at times'; their sculptural treatment developed from trunks to delicate twigs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stems and branches when the architectural idiom allows luxuriant imitation (e.g., porch traceries, angle shafts). Recognize the historical progression—from trunks, to loaded branches, to delicate twigs—and avoid monotonous overuse that can tire the eye or become stylistically obsolete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foliage, flowers, and fruit
rubrics_metrics.description: Foliage, flowers, and fruit are the only organic structures readily capable of being treated independently as ornament; leaf forms are chief sources of subordinate decoration (roots: Greek acanthus, Egyptian lotus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat leaves as fundamental ornamental units: single leaves, outlines, or even hollow foils can provide simple, peaceful charm. Distinguish foliage from stems in design. Use fruit cautiously (often more valuable for color than form) and avoid excessive or gluttonous fruit-decoration associated with certain Renaissance tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Birds as ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Birds possess 'perfect and simple grace' and supplied ornament with representation of spiritual motion via wings; used widely in Byzantine and Lombardic ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor bird forms for elegance and repeats that don't tire the eye. Use bird-of-prey heads and pecking/standing motifs symbolically or decoratively; be mindful of the difficulty of expressing action where musculature is concealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadrupeds and human figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Horses and other quadrupeds are noble sculptural subjects (horses elevated by association with men); the human form is the chief subject of sculpture and sometimes becomes the end of architecture rather than decoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quadrupeds and human figures with consideration of scale and subordination: they can be principal subjects but risk dominating the architecture. Recognize cultural constraints (e.g., Arab abstention from animal forms) and the separate powers of coloration and geometric design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials of ornament are essentially complete
rubrics_metrics.description: The listed materials (leafage, animals, shells, branches, etc.) comprise the sources of ornamental beauty; attempts to draw beauty from other sources generally fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should work within these established material families, using abstract line and color when animal/vegetal imitation is forbidden or unsuitable, as in some Islamic work, but understand such alternatives are different arts (color/geometry rather than imitative sculpture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish treatment modes: expression vs arrangement vs place
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two branches of treatment: expression (how to render the thing) and arrangement (how to place/combine those renderings); separate from the question of place (where on the building to put them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing ornament, first decide how to express the subject (detail level, literalness), then how to arrange repeated elements (symmetry, randomness, limits), and finally the physical placement (capital, shaft, etc.). Treat these as distinct decisions with interdependent effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold evaluative questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Design must answer: (1) How ornament is to be expressed with reference to the mind; (2) How ornament is to be arranged with reference to the sight; (3) How ornament is to be arranged with reference to both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three lenses as a checklist for treatment decisions: cognitive meaning and symbolism (mind), visual composition and perception (sight), and combined effects (both).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must serve the building, not be independent sculpture
rubrics_metrics.description: No perfect piece of sculpture is an architectural ornament except in a vague sense; 'its perfection, in some degree, unfits it for its purpose' as ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating architectural ornament as independent fine art (Titian/Velasquez analogy). Design ornament to be 'beautiful in its place'—subordinate to and aiding the effect of surrounding architectural parts, rather than competing with them in richness or delicacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must be 'beautiful in its place' and subordinate
rubrics_metrics.description: The especial condition of true ornament is that 'it be beautiful in its place, and nowhere else, and that it aid the effect of every portion of the building over which it has influence; that it does not, by its richness, make other parts bald, or, by its delicacy, make other parts coarse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design ornament so its qualities (richness, delicacy, formality) are chosen with relation to its architectural context and use; treat ornament as servant to architecture—formal where needed, silent where needed, hurried where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide extent of subordination vs independence carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: How far ornament may surrender subordination and possess independent will is a difficult question; sometimes apparent archaicism or incapacity produces desirable ornamental effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be critical when using deliberate imperfection or archaic simplification: study examples (illuminated missals, Giotto vs Raphael) to judge how much voluntary abandonment of technical 'power' can be beneficial ornamentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether imperfection is intentional or due to execution
rubrics_metrics.description: In many works it's hard to tell whether 'erroneous' features arise from principle or from 'vulgarity of execution'; such uncertainty complicates prescriptive rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or imitating historical ornament, distinguish intentional abstraction from accidental incompetence; only deliberate, well-considered simplifications should be adopted as stylistic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an overall system appropriate to context and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Three historic systems described: (a) Ninevite/Egyptian resolute abstraction (suited to absolute authorities), (b) Greek system (assumes perfect sculpture/Phidias), (c) Medieval system (inferior details often realized and subordinated by arrangement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a system that fits social and technical realities: avoid attempting a Greek system without great sculptors; prefer the medieval model when working with varying skill levels and the need for broad execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noble abstraction principle
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Noble abstraction' means taking the essential elements of the thing to be represented first, then the rest in order of importance, using any expedient to impress what is wanted on the mind without caring for mere literal accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract and emphasize the core, identifying which features carry the object's spirit (e.g., the 'eyes' of a peacock's tail) and accentuate them (cut in relief, exaggerate) so that the intended character reads correctly at the intended viewing distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for execution by ordinary workmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Architect's business is 'to devise such a system of ornament as shall be capable of execution by uninventive and even unintelligent workmen'—to think for them and indicate expressions the weakest capacity can execute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make ornament legible to simple hands: provide clear, unambiguous forms and mapped-out lines that minimize possibility of error. This allows architecture to be produced at scale (nations' work) rather than limited by need for great sculptors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability constraint: do not demand perfection that limits building
rubrics_metrics.description: With every increase in fastidiousness in execution of ornament you diminish the possible number and grandeur of buildings; greatness is not available in required quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance aspirations for perfect execution with the social/production reality: avoid designs that require a small number of master sculptors; prefer forms that can be reproduced widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three orders of ornament and their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Three orders: (1) servile ornament—executive absolutely subjected to inventive (e.g., great Eastern nations), (2) medieval—inferior workman recognised and guided by ruling mind (described as the truly Christian and only perfect system), (3) ornaments attempting to equalise executive and inventive—Renaissance/revolutionary and destructive of noble architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor the medieval approach (guidance plus scope for inferior workmen) for robust architectural ornament; avoid the Renaissance model that seeks to erase the distinction and thereby undermines architectural nobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realisation vs abstraction: prefer abstraction unless skill permits
rubrics_metrics.description: Realisation (fully naturalistic rendering) is dangerous except under most skilful management; 'abstraction, if true and noble, is almost always more delightful.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realistic, highly finished details only when confident of the executant skill and contextual appropriateness; otherwise adopt true abstraction that captures essential character without literal completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment specifics: expression and arrangement choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment questions include how to express detail (e.g., cut vine-leaf ribs and notches or only general outline?) and how to arrange elements (symmetrically, at random, or unsymmetrically within limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve technical expression before repetition patterns. Choose level of detail according to intended viewing distance, repetition, and relationship to surrounding parts; choose arrangement mode to achieve required subordination or emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of ornament (question of place)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of where ornament is set (e.g., on a capital or on a shaft) is distinct from treatment questions and affects how ornament should be expressed and arranged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide placement early; adapt expression and arrangement to the surface, scale, and function of the element—what suits a capital may be wrong for a shaft, and vice versa.
